sections.text:
They were drawn into this deception also by attention to non-Christian writers, who assign “from which” and “through which” to things distinct from one another by nature. Those writers think that “from which” indicates the material, while “through which” indicates the instrument or, more generally, subordinate agency.

Or rather—for nothing prevents us from taking up their whole account and briefly exposing both its incompatibility with the truth and the inconsistency of these men with their own authorities—those occupied with vain philosophy analyze cause in several ways and divide it according to its proper meanings. Some causes they call initiating; others cooperative or contributory; others they describe as conditions without which something does not occur.

They also assign a special expression to each. The maker is indicated in one way, the instrument in another. For the maker they think “by whom” is appropriate: a bench, for example, is properly said to have been made by the carpenter. To the instrument belongs “through which”: it is made through the adze, the auger, and the other tools. Likewise they make “from which” proper to the material: the product is from wood. “According to which” indicates the conception or model placed before the artisan. Either the craftsman first sketches the object beforehand in his mind and then brings that conception into actuality, or he looks toward an already existing model and directs his work according to its likeness.

They want “for the sake of which” to refer to the end or purpose: the bench is made for human use. “In which” indicates time or place: When was it made? In this time. Where? In this place. Although time and place contribute nothing to the thing being produced, nevertheless production cannot occur without them, since agents require both place and time.

Our opponents learned and admired these distinctions derived from vanity and empty deception and then transferred them to the plain and untechnical teaching of the Spirit, diminishing God the Word and rejecting the Holy Spirit. They did not hesitate to transfer to the Lord of all an expression which outsiders had reserved for lifeless instruments or for the lowest kind of subordinate service—I mean “through whom.” And Christians are not ashamed to assign to the Creator of creation language appropriate to a saw or a hammer.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Basil summarizes philosophical classifications of causality only in order to criticize their rigid transfer into Trinitarian theology.
The contrast between philosophical technical language and the church's scriptural language drives the chapter.
